summary: Gives guidelines for anyone who allocates IPv6 multicast addresses, whether permanent assignments, dynamic allocations, or group identifiers defined in other documents. The goal is to lower the chance that two different groups end up with the same multicast address. It was later updated by RFC 10028.

eli5.summary: When many people name their clubs, two clubs might pick the same name and get confused. These rules say how to hand out group addresses so that no two groups collide.

subtitle: Rules for choosing the low 32 bits of an IPv6 multicast address so different groups do not collide.

tldr.problem: Several link types copy the low 32 bits of an IPv6 multicast address into the link-layer address, so careless choices of those bits can make unrelated groups collide.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC splits the 32-bit group ID space into ranges: IANA-assigned permanent addresses, IANA-assigned permanent group IDs, and a top half for dynamic allocation by servers or hosts. Dynamic addresses also set the T bit.
tldr.outcome: It created an IANA registry of permanent group IDs. It was later updated by RFC 10028.

today: RFC 3307 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 10028, so read the two together.

sections.title: Why Group IDs Need Rules
sections.content:
RFC 3307 specifies guidelines that MUST be followed by any entity that allocates IPv6 multicast addresses. That includes documents or entities assigning permanent addresses, allocating dynamic addresses, or defining permanent multicast group identifiers. The goal is to reduce the chance of address collision, both at the IPv6 layer and at the link layer.

The link-layer problem exists because some media, such as Ethernet (RFC 2464) and FDDI (RFC 2467), take the low-order 32 bits of the IPv6 multicast address, called the group ID, and put them into the link-layer destination address. Group IDs of 32 bits or fewer generate unique link-layer addresses within a given multicast scope.
sections.eli5: If two different groups pick the same short nickname, the mail carrier delivers to both. These rules help pick nicknames that do not clash.

sections.title: Where the Guidelines Apply
sections.content:
The guidelines are meant for any environment where IPv6 multicast addresses are delegated, assigned or selected, and are not limited to MADCAP servers (RFC 2730). The RFC lists several example uses:

  • Source-specific multicast servers can build a group address from a 96-bit prefix (FF3x::/96) plus a group ID.
  • A MADCAP server allocates addresses and creates the group ID using these rules.
  • Nodes in a zeroconf environment generate addresses without central control.
  • IANA can assign permanent multicast addresses for protocol standards requests.
sections.eli5: The rules are not just for one kind of address-giving machine. Anyone who hands out or picks group addresses should follow them.

sections.title: Permanent Addresses and Group IDs
sections.content:
Permanent multicast addresses, like those in RFC 2375, are allocated by IANA. Their group IDs fall in the range 0x00000001 to 0x3FFFFFFF, on an Expert Review basis. Such addresses MUST have the T bit and the P bit set to 0.

Permanent group IDs are a different thing. They identify a service worldwide across many servers, whatever the upper 96 bits of the address are. The RFC's example is NTP with group ID 0x40404040: a client knows that this ID means an NTP multicast stream in any scope. Permanent group IDs are allocated on an Expert Review basis in the range 0x40000000 to 0x7FFFFFFF, for use in addresses defined by RFC 3306.
sections.eli5: Some names are reserved forever, like a famous shop's name. A permanent group ID is a name for a whole service, such as the time service, that works the same everywhere.

sections.title: Dynamic Allocation
sections.content:
Dynamic addresses can come from an allocation server or be chosen by a host. Either way, they MUST have the T bit set to 1, which tells them apart from permanent addresses on media that map the low bits to a link-layer address. The high-order bit of the group ID equals the T flag. For example, permanent FF02::9 maps to Ethernet group address 33-33-00-00-00-09, while dynamic FF32::8000:9 maps to 33-33-80-00-00-09.

Allocation servers (RFC 2730) MUST use group IDs from 0x80000000 to 0xFFFFFFFF. Address management is left to the allocation protocol.

Host-based allocation lets hosts pick their own addresses. The group ID is a pseudo-random 32-bit number, or one made following RFC 1750, and MUST fall in 0x80000000 to 0xFFFFFFFF, which can be done by setting the high-order bit to 1. Collision detection and claim notification are left to the protocol in use.
sections.eli5: For temporary names, a helper can give you one, or you can pick your own. Either way it must come from the upper half of the list, so it never steps on a permanent name.

sections.title: IANA Registry and Ranges
sections.content:
The RFC asks IANA to create a new registry of permanent group ID values, so they can be used across multiple domains using the RFC 3306 address architecture. It also sets allocation rules, following RFC 2434. Permanent addresses with a matching IPv4 multicast address use group IDs 1 to 0x3FFFFFFF, and IPv6-only permanent addresses use 0x100 to 0x3FFFFFFF, both on an Expert Review basis. Permanent group IDs use 0x40000000 to 0x7FFFFFFF. The range 0x80000000 to 0xFFFFFFFF is reserved for dynamic allocation.

Every approved request for a permanent IPv6 multicast address gets a unique group ID that is reserved in all valid IPv6 multicast scopes.
sections.eli5: The official keeper writes a ledger of permanent names. Each name is held in every neighborhood at once so nobody else can reuse it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The allocation mechanisms do not change the security properties of the Any Source or Source Specific multicast service models of IPv4 and IPv6. The RFC does warn that the potential to allocate large blocks of addresses can lead to Denial-of-Service attacks, and points to RFC 2908 for a deeper discussion of security issues in dynamic allocation.
sections.eli5: Handing out names does not make anything safer or less safe. The one worry is someone grabbing a huge pile of names so nobody else can have any.
